newsitem.title: USA: Rangebound US session yields slightly lower dollar.
newsitem.headline: Rangebound US session yields slightly lower dollar.

text.p: A fatigued dollar edged modestly lower in a rangebound U.S. session on Thursday, holding on to some of its overseas gains but failing repeatedly to push back above the 1.80 mark level.
Providing mild mark support against the dollar were remarks from Bundesbank Presdident Hans Tietmeyer and signs from Germany's Finance Ministry that it will take a hard-line on meeting EMU criteria.
Continuous but unsubstantiated talk that European central banks were propping up the German currency also weighed on the uncharacteristically sluggish dollar/mark rate.
"Whether the central banks are there are not, from a technical perspective the dollar looks tired," said Kevin Lawrie, global foreign exchange manager at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
The dollar ended at 1.7915/25 marks, below its opening rate of 1.7950/60. The greenback also fell modestly to 115.85/95 yen from 116.15/25 at the outset of trading.

Tietmeyer said on Thursday that he hoped the current upward "correction" of the dollar against the mark would not go too far and warned that officials were watching developments in the foreign exchange market closely.
Traders bought the mark on the remarks, setting of stop-loss sell orders that pushed dollar/mark below 1.79. But the losses were well contained and the rate bounced off support at 1.7870.

Dealers said Tietmeyer's remarks were not strong enough to convince the market that Germany is really willing to defend its currency at a time when mark weakness is boosting domestic exports and growth.
They cited comments from a German government spokesman, who said on Wednesday that there was no need to "dramatize" recent currency movements.

"It seems quite clear that the Bundesbank is trying to get across to the market that they are watching foreign exchange rates carefully, but are not going to try to draw a line in the sand," said Bob Savage, chief dealer at Lehman Brothers.
Nevertheless, Savage said that the dollar's repeated inability to hold above the 1.80 mark level indicated that that was "the line to watch."
Contributing to dollar/mark's sluggish performance during the U.S. session were comments from senior German Finance Ministry official Hansgeorg Hauser.
Hauser said in a speech in Duesseldorf that Germany would insist on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty when it came to choosing qualified countries for Europe's planned single currency.

Against the yen, the dollar traded above the 116 threshold for much of the day, retaining gains made overseas after Japan's Ministry of Finance reported smaller-than-expected gains in the country's June trade surplus.
The data showed that its overall surplus rose by 27.7 percent year-over-year to 934.21 billion yen while its surplus with the U.S. climbed 26.8 percent to 373.14 billion yen.

"The Japanese surplus went up handily, however the market was anticipating a much larger increase and it was a buyer of dollars and seller of yen on the news," said Susan Stearns, director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal.
Keeping dollar losses in check on Thursday was more good news on the U.S. economy.

The Philadelphia Federal Reserve reported that its July business index, a key indicator of activity in the manufacturing sector, rose to 28.1 in July, up from 25.2 in June, and much higher than the market had expected.
Housing starts also pushed up a healthy 4.8 percent in June to a 1.452 million unit annual rate, with the multi-family sector showing a sizable 12.9 percent advance.

Dealers said the release of Germany's closely watched Ifo business indices for June and the Commerce Department's report on U.S. May international trade should garner a great deal of attention on Friday.
In other trade on Thursday, the dollar fell slightly to 1.4800/10 Swiss francs from 1.4808/18 at the open and climbed to Canadian $1.3765/70 from C$1.3731/36.
The pound pushed back above 3.0 marks and rose to $1.6725/35 from $1.6653/58, while the Australian dollar edged up to $0.7363/68 from $0.7360/65.
(( -- Noah Barkin, N.A. Forex Unit, 212-859-1673 ))
